headline: High-risk shared-workspace and unsandboxed flow execution create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a content-writing repository with no runtime isolation or I/O surfaces documented, while agent B has server-side flows, file I/O, and can chain multiple agents. If A’s content is fed into B’s flow nodes or files, B may treat attacker-controlled text as instructions. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF agent A content is imported into a Langflow node or uploaded file
IF agent B parses that content as prompt or tool instructions
mitigations: Restrict B to trusted inputs only for the flow
Add a manual review step before any A-derived text reaches B
Disable or isolate file-uploaded prompt sources in B
requires-engineering: add provenance tags between A outputs and B inputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B explicitly reads and writes the filesystem and handles flow inputs, intermediate outputs, and per-flow credentials; agent A is a repository of prompt-engineering content that could be stored in shared files or uploads. A shared workspace can expose B’s stored secrets or intermediate outputs to A-derived content handling. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default deployments, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents access the same server filesystem or uploaded-file workspace
IF B stores flow credentials or intermediate outputs in that workspace
mitigations: Separate A and B into distinct directories or containers
Move B secrets out of shared files immediately
Audit uploaded files for sensitive content before reuse
requires-engineering: enforce workspace ACLs and secret redaction

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write the filesystem; agent A is a repository artifact with no runtime capabilities, but if A is used as a source tree or shared workspace, B’s writes can collide with A-managed files. Because B’s concurrency model uses shared server-side state, conflicts are plausible even though A itself is non-runnable. Uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF B writes into a directory also used to store A’s repository files
IF multiple B instances operate on the same shared state or store
mitigations: Use separate working directories per agent
Avoid concurrent writes to shared stores
Serialize file-mutating steps in B
requires-engineering: add locking around shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B’s graph-based flows can chain multiple agents and tools, and its Python code component is unsandboxed by default. If A’s prompt-engineering content is used as authoritative guidance or embedded instructions, B may propagate errors into downstream actions or tool calls without verification. The blast radius can extend across multiple flow steps, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF A-derived text is used as an instruction source inside a B flow
IF B downstream nodes act on that text without verification
mitigations: Insert a verification node before any action-taking step
Require citations or structured schemas for A-derived content
Disable unsandboxed Python components for untrusted flows
requires-engineering: add policy checks between flow nodes

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B stores per-flow component credentials and processes flow inputs/intermediate outputs, while agent A is a public open-source repository with no sensitive data class documented. No residency or regulated-data mismatch is evidenced here, so only a low compliance concern remains from generic retention/logging ambiguity. A is cited for being public/open-source; B is cited for credential handling.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into B flows
IF B retention or logging exceeds the operator’s policy
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in B flows
Review B retention settings before use
Purge stored credentials after each run
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
